lessons.title: What Borrowing Really Means: Principal, Interest, Tenure and Security

children.text: "We got the loan at 9.5%." Every founder and finance manager has said some version of this, as though one number describes the deal. It does not. Two loans at 9.5% can be wildly different arrangements: one repayable over three years against the factory, the other over eight years with a personal guarantee from the promoter and a clause letting the bank recall the whole amount if profits fall.
This lesson takes a loan apart into the pieces that actually matter.

body.text: A loan is not money rented at a rate. It is a set of promises: how much you took, how long you have, what you pay each month, what the lender can seize if you stop, and who pays if the company cannot.

children.text: The Four Variables

body.caption: What every loan agreement is really specifying

cells: Principal
How much you owe, regardless of business performance
Is this sized to what we need, or to what the bank will give?
Interest rate
What the money costs each year
Is it fixed or floating, and what benchmark is it linked to?
Tenure
How long you have, and therefore the size of each instalment
Does this match the life of the asset we are funding?
Security
What the lender takes if you default
What exactly is charged, and is a personal guarantee involved?

children.text: Two more sit underneath: the repayment structure, meaning how the money flows back, and the covenants, meaning the conditions you must keep meeting. Covenants get their own lesson later in this chapter.
Tenure: The Variable People Get Wrong
A longer
tenure
makes the monthly number smaller and the total number much bigger. Take a ₹50 lakh term loan at 10% a year.

markDefs.definition: The period over which a loan is repaid. A longer tenure lowers each instalment and raises the total interest paid.

body.caption: P is the principal, r is the monthly interest rate and n is the number of months
The same ₹50 lakh loan at 10%, over two tenures

cells: Monthly EMI
Total paid over the loan
Total interest

stats.label: Interest more than doubles
stats.context: The price of the smaller EMI

body.title: The cost of stretching
body.prompt: The ₹50 lakh loan at 10% over 5 years has an EMI of ₹1,06,235. Over the full 60 months, how much interest is paid in total, in ₹ lakh? Answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: ₹1,06,235 times 60 months is about ₹63.74 lakh. Less the ₹50 lakh borrowed, that is about ₹13.7 lakh of interest. Over ten years the same loan costs about ₹29.3 lakh in interest, which is more than double for the same principal.

children.text: Change the tenure in the calculator above and watch the two numbers move in opposite directions. Then apply the rule that matters: match the tenure to the life of the asset. A machine that will run for eight years can carry a longer loan. Funding three months of inventory with a five-year loan means you are still paying for stock you sold years ago.

body.text: A lower EMI is not a cheaper loan. Relationship managers know that most borrowers compare monthly instalments, so stretching the tenure is the easiest way to make an expensive loan feel affordable. Always ask for the total interest over the life of the loan, in rupees.

children.text: How Indian Lenders Actually Set Your Rate
Bank lending rates in India are not invented deal by deal. They are built from a benchmark plus a spread.
The RBI repo rate
is the policy anchor. It stood at 5.25% through the middle of 2026.
The benchmark.

Retail and MSE loans are typically linked to an external benchmark, usually the repo rate itself, giving an external benchmark lending rate. Larger corporate loans are often linked to the bank's marginal cost of funds based lending rate, or MCLR.
The spread
is what the bank adds for your credit risk, the security you offer, the tenure and its own margin. This is the part you negotiate.

body.caption: Only the spread is specific to you, and only the spread is negotiable

stats.label: Illustrative spread
stats.context: Credit risk, security, tenure, bank margin

body.text: On a repo-linked floating rate loan, an RBI rate cut reaches you automatically at the next reset, and so does a rate hike. On a fixed rate loan neither does. Floating is usually cheaper over a full cycle, but it moves your interest cost without asking, which matters if your margins are thin.

body.title: What you negotiate
body.textWithBlank: In a benchmark-linked loan, the borrower cannot change the benchmark, so the part that is actually negotiable is the ___.
body.explanation: The benchmark is set by the RBI or by the bank's own cost of funds. The spread reflects how risky the bank thinks you are, which improves with a better credit history, stronger financials and better security.

children.text: Repayment Structures
How the money flows back is a separate decision from how much it costs, and it can matter more to survival.

body.caption: Four ways a loan is repaid

cells: Equated instalments (EMI)
The same amount every month, part interest and part principal
Assets that start generating cash immediately
Bullet repayment
Interest during the term, the entire principal at the end
Bonds and short-term borrowing where a refinancing or inflow is expected
Moratorium then instalments
No principal, sometimes no interest, for an agreed initial period
Projects with a construction or ramp-up period
Structured or ballooning
Small instalments early, larger later, matched to a cash flow forecast
Infrastructure and long-gestation projects

children.text: A
moratorium
is not free money. Interest usually keeps accruing and is added to what you owe, so the loan grows during the quiet period. Ask specifically whether interest is waived or merely deferred.

markDefs.definition: An agreed period at the start of a loan during which no principal, and sometimes no interest, is repaid.

children.text: Security: What the Lender Takes If You Stop Paying
Indian lenders distinguish primary security, which is the asset being funded, from collateral, which is everything else pledged to make the lender comfortable.

body.caption: Forms of security in Indian lending

cells: Hypothecation
Movable assets: stock, machinery, vehicles, receivables
The borrower keeps and uses them
Mortgage
Immovable property: land, buildings, factory premises
The borrower keeps possession, the title is charged
Pledge
Movable assets handed over, such as shares or goods in a warehouse
The lender or its agent holds them
Personal guarantee
The personal assets of a promoter or director
Not an asset charge at all, a personal promise
Corporate guarantee
The assets and cash flows of a group company
The guaranteeing company continues as normal

children.text: When a company creates a charge over its assets, it must register that charge with the Registrar of Companies, generally within 30 days, under the Companies Act, 2013. Registered charges are publicly visible on the MCA portal, which is how a second lender discovers that your machinery is already pledged elsewhere.

body.text: A [[personal guarantee]] undoes the main benefit of running a limited company. If the business fails, the lender can pursue the promoter's own house and savings, and under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code personal guarantors can be proceeded against directly. Treat it as the most expensive thing in the term sheet, not a formality at the end.

body.title: Match the loan to the need
body.question: A Surat textile unit needs ₹80 lakh to buy fabric for orders that will be delivered and paid for within four months. Which structure fits best?
options: A ten-year term loan with a mortgage on the promoter's house
A short-term working capital facility such as cash credit, secured by hypothecation of stock and receivables
A bullet loan repayable in seven years
body.explanation: The need is short and self-liquidating: the stock converts to cash within months. A working capital facility secured by that very stock and the resulting receivables matches the cash cycle. A ten-year loan against the promoter's house would still be running long after the fabric was sold.

children.text: The Costs That Are Not the Interest Rate
The rate is the largest cost, not the only one. Before comparing two offers, add these up.
Processing fee
, often 0.25% to 1% of the sanctioned amount, sometimes negotiable to nil.
Documentation, stamp duty and mortgage creation charges
, which vary by state and can be significant on property.
Valuation and legal fees
for the security offered.
Insurance
on the hypothecated or mortgaged asset, usually mandatory.
Annual review or renewal fees
on working capital limits.
Commitment charges
on the undrawn portion of a sanctioned limit.
Prepayment or foreclosure charges
, which is where the rules recently changed.

body.label: Prepayment charges: what changed in India
body.context: Issued on 2 July 2025 and applying to loans sanctioned or renewed on or after 1 January 2026, these directions bar regulated lenders from levying pre-payment or foreclosure charges on floating rate loans to individuals for non-business purposes, and extend protection to micro and small enterprises. Conditions and limits apply by lender category and loan type, so check the applicable position for your specific facility.

body.title: Fund-based and non-fund-based: a distinction that confuses everyone

children.text: Not everything a bank sanctions involves handing over cash.
Fund-based limits
put money in your account: term loans, cash credit, overdrafts, working capital demand loans, bill discounting.
Non-fund-based limits
lend the bank's name rather than its money: a letter of credit tells your supplier the bank will pay if you do not, and a bank guarantee does the same for a contractual obligation.

Non-fund-based limits cost a commission rather than interest, which makes them look cheap. They are still exposure: if the bank has to pay out under a guarantee or letter of credit, that amount immediately becomes a loan you owe, usually at a penal rate. Many companies have discovered the true cost of a bank guarantee only on the day it was invoked.

body.title: Compare the offers
body.question: Bank A offers ₹2 crore at 9.5% for 5 years with a 1% processing fee and no prepayment charge. Bank B offers 9.1% for 5 years with a 0.25% processing fee, but a 2% prepayment charge and a requirement for a personal guarantee from the promoter. The company expects a large inflow in year 3 and wants to repay early. What should it weigh most heavily?
options: Only the interest rate, so Bank B wins
The prepayment charge and the personal guarantee, which together can outweigh the 0.4% rate saving
The processing fee, which is the biggest difference
Neither, since both offers are effectively identical
body.explanation: A 0.4% rate difference on ₹2 crore is roughly ₹80,000 a year before the loan starts amortising. A 2% prepayment charge on an early repayment could cost well over a lakh in one go, and the personal guarantee exposes the promoter's own assets. Cheapest headline rate and cheapest loan are not the same thing.

body.title: Reading a sanction letter properly
body.scenario: You handle finance at a Rajkot engineering firm. The bank has sanctioned ₹3 crore: a ₹2 crore term loan at repo plus 3.9% floating, repayable over 7 years with a 6-month moratorium, and a ₹1 crore cash credit limit renewable annually. Security is hypothecation of plant and machinery and stock, a mortgage on the factory land, and personal guarantees from both directors. There is a 0.5% processing fee and a 1% commitment charge on the undrawn portion of the cash credit.
body.prompt: What would you check, question or negotiate before signing?
body.modelAnswer:
On pricing:
1. Confirm what the spread is over which benchmark, how often the rate resets, and whether the spread can be revised by the bank during the tenure or is fixed for the life of the loan.
2. Ask for the total interest in rupees over 7 years at the current rate, and at 2 percentage points higher, so the board sees the sensitivity.
3. Negotiate the processing fee. On ₹3 crore, 0.5% is ₹1.5 lakh, and this is one of the most commonly waived items.
4. Question the 1% commitment charge on the undrawn cash credit. Either size the limit realistically or push for the charge to be dropped, otherwise you are paying to not borrow.

On the moratorium:
5. Establish whether interest is waived during the 6 months or merely deferred and added to the principal. Almost always the latter, which quietly increases what you repay.
6. Check the machinery is actually generating cash by month 7, when instalments begin.

On security:
7. The bank has taken plant, stock and the factory land, and then personal guarantees on top. Ask what release the guarantees have: do they fall away once the loan is, say, half repaid, or when a financial ratio is met?
8. Ensure the charge is registered with the Registrar of Companies within the statutory period, and get the charge documents on file.
9. Ask whether the security is exclusive to this bank, which will constrain your ability to borrow from anyone else later.

On flexibility:
10. Confirm the prepayment position in writing, given the RBI directions on floating rate loans, and whether your facility falls within them.
11. Read the recall and cross-default clauses. A clause letting the bank recall the term loan if the cash credit account is irregular can turn a small working capital problem into a ₹3 crore demand.

body.title: Before signing any loan document
steps: What is the total interest in rupees over the full tenure, not just the rate?
Is the rate fixed or floating, and if floating, linked to what benchmark and reset how often?
Does the tenure match the life of the asset being funded?
What exactly is charged as security, and is any of it personal?
Is there a moratorium, and does interest accrue during it?
What are the processing, commitment, renewal and prepayment charges?
Under what conditions can the lender recall the loan early?
Has the charge been registered with the Registrar of Companies on time?

body.label: Reserve Bank of India
body.description: The source for the current repo rate, lending rate guidelines and circulars such as the 2025 directions on pre-payment charges. Check the current policy rate here before relying on any figure quoted in a lesson or a sales pitch.

cards.definition: The amount borrowed, repayable in full whatever the business does.
The repayment period. Longer tenure means a smaller EMI and much higher total interest.
External benchmark lending rate, typically the repo rate plus the bank's spread.
Marginal cost of funds based lending rate, the internal benchmark used for many corporate loans.
A charge over movable assets that the borrower continues to possess and use.
A charge over immovable property such as land or buildings.
An initial period with no principal repayment. Interest usually still accrues.
A letter of credit or bank guarantee, where the bank lends its name, not cash, until it is invoked.

points: A loan is four decisions, not one rate: principal, interest, tenure and security.
Stretching the tenure lowers the EMI and sharply raises total interest. On ₹50 lakh at 10%, moving from 5 to 10 years more than doubles interest paid.
Indian bank rates are a benchmark plus a spread, and only the spread is negotiable.
Match the tenure to the life of the asset. Short needs get working capital facilities, long assets get term loans.
Security can be hypothecation, mortgage, pledge or a guarantee, and charges must be registered with the Registrar of Companies.
A personal guarantee undoes limited liability and should be treated as the most expensive clause in the document.
Processing fees, commitment charges, insurance and prepayment terms can outweigh a small difference in interest rate.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or tax advice. Rates, spreads and fees are illustrative and vary by lender, borrower and date. The repo rate quoted was current in mid-2026 and changes with RBI policy. Regulatory positions, including on prepayment charges, change over time, so verify current rules with your lender or on the RBI website.
